29733.m: Biel/Bienne is the largest bilingual town in Switzerland.

29734.q: How many Swiss cantons are officially bilingual in German and French?
29734.e: They are the cantons of Bern, Fribourg and Valais. The Grisons is trilingual, with German, Romansh and Italian.
29734.m: Bern, Fribourg and Valais are bilingual cantons.

29735.q: In which part of Valais do most people speak French?
29735.e: In the lower, western part of Valais people mainly speak French. In Upper Valais, which includes the Goms and the Saas valley, people speak German.
29735.m: In Lower Valais people speak French, in Upper Valais German.

29736.q: How did the German-French language border in Switzerland come about?
29736.e: In the early Middle Ages the language of the Alemanni spread, while in the west people spoke a Romance language. So the border gradually took shape.
29736.m: The language border grew over centuries.

29737.q: Which small town in the canton of Fribourg is mainly German-speaking?
29737.e: Murten (in French Morat) lies close to the language border. Most of its people speak German.
29737.m: Murten is a German-speaking town in the bilingual canton of Fribourg.

29738.q: On which day is St Gall’s Day celebrated?
29738.e: St Gall’s Day marks the day the saint died. In the past it was an important date in the countryside, for example for markets and paying interest.
29738.m: St Gall’s Day is on 16 October.

29739.q: According to tradition, which country did the monk Gallus come from?
29739.e: According to tradition Gallus came from Ireland. As a monk he travelled through France as far as Lake Constance.
29739.m: According to tradition Gallus came from Ireland.

29740.q: How did Gallus live in the area of present-day St Gallen?
a: As a hermit in a cell in the forest
As a king in a castle
As a trader in a town
As a farmer on a big farm
29740.e: Gallus built himself a simple cell in the forest and lived there as a hermit. The town of St Gallen later grew from this place.
29740.m: Gallus lived as a hermit in the forest.

29741.q: According to tradition, how did Columbanus and Gallus deal with the pagan idols of the Alemanni?
a: They put them up in churches
29741.e: The accounts of their lives report that Gallus destroyed idols in Tuggen and Bregenz or threw them into the lake. This turned the locals against the monks.
29741.m: Gallus fought against the old Alemannic belief in gods.

29742.q: According to legend, which animal brought Gallus wood while he was building his cell?
29742.e: Gallus is said to have told the animal to put wood on the fire and given it bread in return. That is why the coat of arms of the city of St Gallen shows this animal.
29742.m: According to legend a bear helped St Gallus.

29743.q: What was founded at the grave of Gallus in 719?
29743.e: The priest Otmar founded a monastery at the grave of Gallus. The town of St Gallen later grew up around the monastery.
29743.m: The Abbey of St Gall grew up at the grave of Gallus.

29744.q: What in St Gallen is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
a: The Abbey District with cathedral and library
29744.e: The Abbey District is the former monastery of Gallus. With the cathedral and the famous Abbey Library, it has been a World Heritage Site since 1983.
29744.m: The Abbey District of St Gallen is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

29745.q: Who ruled large areas of present-day eastern Switzerland from the Abbey of St Gall until 1798?
29745.e: The abbot of St Gall also ruled as a worldly lord. That is why he was called the Prince-Abbot. In 1805 the monastery was dissolved.
29745.m: The Prince-Abbot of St Gall ruled over large parts of eastern Switzerland.

29746.q: Which building on the Plan of St Gall is drawn largest and most precisely?
29746.e: The church forms the centre of the whole complex. It is drawn especially carefully, with altars and measurements.
29746.m: The great church stands at the centre of the monastery plan.

29747.q: Around which year was the Plan of St Gall made?
29747.e: Experts date the plan to about 819 to 837, usually around 825/826. So it comes from the Carolingian period.
29747.m: The monastery plan comes from the early 9th century.

29748.q: What material is the Plan of St Gall drawn on?
29748.e: The plan consists of five pieces of parchment, that is treated animal skin, sewn together. It measures about 112 by 77 centimetres.
29748.m: The monastery plan is drawn on parchment.

29749.q: Roughly how many buildings are drawn on the Plan of St Gall?
29749.e: The plan contains floor plans of about 50 buildings with 333 labels. The complex would have had room for over 100 monks.
29749.m: About fifty buildings can be seen on the monastery plan.

29750.q: How is the cemetery designed on the Plan of St Gall?
29750.e: Fruit trees are drawn between the graves. In this way the plan links the place of the dead with a picture of the garden of paradise.
29750.m: On the monastery plan the cemetery is also an orchard.

29751.q: What was the Plan of St Gall meant for?
a: As a model for an ideal monastery
As a map of eastern Switzerland
As a plan for building a castle
As a street map of St Gallen
29751.e: The plan shows what a perfect monastery with a church, workshops, gardens and stables could look like. But it was never built exactly like this.
29751.m: The monastery plan shows an ideal monastery.

29752.q: Roughly how old is the Abbey of Saint-Maurice in Valais?
29752.e: The abbey was founded in 515. In 2015 it celebrated 1,500 years.
29752.m: The Abbey of Saint-Maurice is over 1,500 years old.

29753.q: In which canton is the Abbey of Saint-Maurice?
29753.e: The Abbey of Saint-Maurice lies in the Rhône valley in the canton of Valais. It was founded in 515.
29753.m: The Abbey of Saint-Maurice is in Valais.

29754.q: Which saint is the Abbey of Saint-Maurice named after?
29754.e: Maurice and his soldiers are said to have died as martyrs here. The French name Maurice comes from the Latin Mauritius.
29754.m: The Abbey of Saint-Maurice bears the name of St Maurice.

29755.q: According to the legend of Saint-Maurice, who was St Maurice?
29755.e: According to legend, Maurice led a Roman troop. He and his soldiers are said to have been killed because, as Christians, they would not obey.
29755.m: According to legend, Maurice was a Roman soldier and a Christian.

29756.q: Who had a post at Saint-Maurice long before the monastery?
29756.e: The Romans had a customs and military post here at a narrow point in the Rhône valley. The place was called Agaunum then.
29756.m: Saint-Maurice was already an important place in Roman times.

29757.q: What is the Abbey of Saint-Maurice especially known for?
a: Oldest continuously existing monastery in the West
29757.e: Since it was founded, a religious community has lived at Saint-Maurice without a break. Today it is the Augustinian Canons.
29757.m: Saint-Maurice is seen as the oldest continuously inhabited monastery in the West.

29758.q: What did the monks at Saint-Maurice once do day and night without stopping?
29758.e: The monks took turns in groups, so that singing and prayer in praise of God never stopped. This was called laus perennis.
29758.m: At Saint-Maurice monks once sang and prayed without a break.

29759.q: Which neighbouring country borders the Val Müstair, where St John’s Abbey lies?
29759.e: The Val Müstair lies at the far eastern end of Switzerland. Just after the village of Müstair, South Tyrol begins, which belongs to Italy.
29759.m: Müstair Abbey lies close to the border with Italy.

29761.q: According to tradition, which ruler founded Müstair Abbey?
29761.e: Legend says Charlemagne founded the abbey. A life-size statue of him stands in the church.
29761.m: Charlemagne is seen as the founder of Müstair Abbey.

29762.q: What is the abbey church of Müstair world-famous for?
a: The largest stained-glass windows in Europe
29762.e: Many frescoes with scenes from the Carolingian period survive in the church. There are hardly so many early wall paintings anywhere else.
29762.m: Müstair has unique wall paintings from the Carolingian period.

29763.q: How were experts able to work out the exact founding date of Müstair Abbey?
a: From the tree rings in the building timber
From a coin in the foundations
From an inscription on the doorway
29763.e: Dendrochronology compares the width of the tree rings in wood with known patterns. That way you know when a tree was cut down.
29763.m: Tree rings in wood reveal the age of buildings.

29764.q: Who lives in St John’s Abbey in Müstair today?
29764.e: At first the abbey was a monastery for men. Since the 12th century nuns have lived there following the Rule of St Benedict.
29764.m: Benedictine nuns live in Müstair today.

29765.q: What is housed today in the medieval Planta Tower of Müstair Abbey?
29765.e: The tower was built around 960 and later extended by Abbess Angelina von Planta. Today the abbey museum there shows the history of the abbey.
29765.m: The Planta Tower houses the Müstair Abbey museum.

29766.q: Which hermit lived in the 9th century in the Dark Forest, where Einsiedeln Abbey later grew up?
29766.e: Meinrad was a monk from Reichenau who withdrew into solitude. He is seen as the spiritual founder of Einsiedeln.
29766.m: St Meinrad lived as a hermit where Einsiedeln Abbey later stood.

29767.q: How did the hermit Meinrad die?
29767.e: Two robbers killed Meinrad in 861. Since then he has been honoured as a martyr.

29768.q: According to legend, which animals followed Meinrad’s murderers?
29768.e: The birds gave away the killers, who were then caught. That is why the abbey and the village of Einsiedeln have these animals on their coat of arms.
29768.m: Two ravens are the heraldic animals of Einsiedeln.

29769.q: Which monastic rule do the monks of Einsiedeln Abbey live by?
29769.e: In 934 Eberhard from Strasbourg gathered the hermits into a community following Benedict’s rule. Einsiedeln is still a Benedictine monastery today.

29770.q: Who destroyed the Chapel of Grace in Einsiedeln in 1798?
29770.e: When the French marched into Switzerland in 1798, the chapel got torn down. It got rebuilt from 1815 to 1817.
29770.m: The Chapel of Grace in Einsiedeln was destroyed in 1798 and later rebuilt.

29771.q: In which architectural style was Einsiedeln Abbey rebuilt from 1704?
29771.e: Brother Caspar Moosbrugger planned the huge Baroque complex. The abbey church was consecrated in 1735.
29771.m: Einsiedeln Abbey is a Baroque building.

29772.q: Who attacked Einsiedeln Abbey in January 1314 in the so-called March Dispute?
29772.e: Schwyz and the abbey argued for a long time about pastures and forests. In 1314 men from Schwyz plundered the abbey and took monks prisoner.
29772.m: In the March Dispute, Schwyz and Einsiedeln Abbey fought over land.

29773.q: Through which narrow gorge in the canton of Uri does the route to the Gotthard lead?
29773.e: Only a bridge in the Schöllenen Gorge made the Gotthard route passable. According to legend, the Devil built the Devil’s Bridge.
29773.m: The route to the Gotthard leads through the Schöllenen Gorge.

29774.q: What already stood at the top of the Gotthard Pass in the Middle Ages to take in travellers?
29774.e: A hospice is a simple inn for travellers. On the Gotthard, muleteers and pilgrims found shelter there from cold and storms.
29774.m: On the Gotthard a hospice gave travellers shelter.

29775.q: Which big trading city in northern Italy could traders from the north reach especially directly over the Gotthard?
29775.e: From the Gotthard the route leads down through Ticino into Lombardy. Milan was the most important trading city there.
29775.m: Over the Gotthard you reached Milan directly.

29776.q: What were the men called who took goods over the alpine passes with mules and horses?
29776.e: A pack animal carries loads on its back. The muleteers led such animals in lines over the passes.
29776.m: Muleteers took goods over the passes with pack animals.

29777.q: Which village in Ticino lies on the south side of the Gotthard Pass?
29777.e: From the top of the pass the road leads down to Airolo in the Leventina valley. Andermatt and Göschenen are on the Uri side.
29777.m: Airolo lies on the south side of the Gotthard.

29778.q: Which saint is the Gotthard named after?
29778.e: At the top of the pass stood a chapel for St Godehard, a Bishop of Hildesheim. The name Gotthard comes from his name.
29778.m: The Gotthard bears the name of St Godehard.

29780.q: In the legend, what payment did the Devil demand for building the bridge?
a: the soul of the first to cross
a sack full of gold and silver
half of all the harvests in the valley
29780.e: The Devil wanted the soul of the first creature to cross the bridge. That was his price for the work.
29780.m: The Devil demanded the first soul on the bridge.

29781.q: In the legend, how did the people of Uri trick the Devil?
a: They let an animal cross first
They tore the bridge down at once
They rang all the church bells
29781.e: Instead of a person, the people of Uri sent an animal across the bridge. So the Devil did not get a human soul.
29781.m: The people of Uri sent an animal across the bridge first.

29782.q: In the legend, what is the boulder called that the Devil wanted to hurl at the bridge in anger?
29782.e: According to legend, the Devil was driven away with a cross, and the stone missed the bridge. The Devil’s Stone lies near Göschenen and was moved in the 1970s for road building.
29782.m: The Devil’s Stone recalls the legend of the Devil’s Bridge.

29783.q: Why was the route through the Schöllenen Gorge so dangerous in the past?
a: Because of steep rock walls and the wild Reuss
Because of many robbers in the forest
29783.e: In the narrow gorge the Reuss rushes down between steep rocks. Only bridges and walkways made the route to the Gotthard passable.
29783.m: The Schöllenen is a narrow, wild gorge of the Reuss.

29784.q: What material did people use for the first Devil’s Bridge?
29784.e: The first bridge over the Reuss had been built of wood. Later a stone bridge replaced it.
29784.m: The first Devil’s Bridge: made of wood.

29785.q: Which town did Duke Berthold V of Zähringen found in 1191?
29785.e: Berthold V had the town built on a well-protected site. It later became the most powerful city of the Confederation.
29785.m: Berthold V of Zähringen founded the town of Bern in 1191.

29786.q: According to legend, which animal is Bern named after?
29786.e: According to legend, the first animal Berthold V killed while hunting was a bear. That is why Bern also has a bear on its coat of arms.
29786.m: Bern is said to be named after the bear.

29787.q: What is the name of the fountain in Bern’s old town that remembers the family who founded the city?
29787.e: The fountain remembers the dukes who founded the city. It stands in the Kramgasse and dates from the 16th century.
29787.m: The Zähringer Fountain in Bern remembers the founders of the city.

29788.q: In which year did the House of Zähringen die out with Berthold V?
29788.e: Berthold V had no sons. With his death in 1218 the House of Zähringen came to an end, and his lands were divided up.
29788.m: The House of Zähringen died out in 1218.

29789.q: Which town on the lake of the same name is a Zähringer town?
29789.e: Murten was laid out as a town by the Zähringers in the 12th century. It is one of the Zähringer towns.

29790.q: Why did the Zähringers found new towns?
a: To secure their rule and trade
To build ports for seagoing ships
29790.e: Towns with walls protected roads and river crossings. Markets also brought the lords taxes and tolls.
29790.m: The Zähringers used towns to secure their rule and trade.

29791.q: Where did the Zähringer family originally come from?
29791.e: Zähringen Castle lies near Freiburg im Breisgau. From there the dukes also founded towns in what is now Switzerland.
29791.m: The Zähringers came from southern Germany.

29792.q: In which present-day canton is Kyburg Castle, after which the Counts of Kyburg named themselves?
29792.e: Kyburg Castle lies near Winterthur. The powerful family of counts took its name from this castle.
29792.m: Kyburg Castle is in the canton of Zurich.

29793.q: Which family took over the large lands of the Kyburgs after they died out?
29793.e: The only heiress was a child. Her guardian belonged to this family and brought the inheritance to his house.
29793.m: The Kyburg inheritance went to the Habsburgs.

29794.q: Which future king became the guardian of Anna, the Kyburg heiress?
29794.e: Rudolf’s mother was a Kyburg. As guardian he managed the inheritance, and in 1273 he became King of the Romans.
29794.m: Rudolf of Habsburg managed the Kyburg inheritance.

29795.q: Which town in Central Switzerland was founded by the Kyburgs?
29795.e: Zug lies on Lake Zug and was laid out as a town by the Counts of Kyburg. Later it passed to the Habsburgs.
29795.m: The Kyburgs founded the town of Zug.

29796.q: Which town on the Limmat with hot springs did the Kyburgs found around 1230?
29796.e: Baden was already known in Roman times for its thermal springs. The Kyburgs founded a town there around 1230.
29796.m: Baden was founded by the Kyburgs.

29797.q: Why did the power of the Counts of Kyburg end around 1264?
a: There were no more male heirs
They lost a battle against Bern
29797.e: Hartmann V died in 1263 and Hartmann IV in 1264. After that there were no more male Kyburgs, and the inheritance went to the Habsburgs.

29798.q: What is Kyburg Castle near Winterthur today?
29798.e: Kyburg Castle belongs to the canton of Zurich. In the museum you can find out how people lived in a castle in the Middle Ages.
29798.m: Kyburg Castle is a museum today.

29799.q: What did it mean for an area to have imperial freedom?
a: It was directly under the king
It could choose its own king
It no longer belonged to any empire
29799.e: Areas with imperial freedom had no count or duke above them. They were answerable only to the king or emperor.
29799.m: Areas with imperial freedom were directly under the king.

29800.q: Which of the Forest Cantons was the first to receive a charter of freedom, in 1231?
29800.e: Uri lay on the route to the Gotthard, which was important for the empire. That is why the king took the valley under his direct rule.
29800.m: Uri was the first of the Forest Cantons to receive imperial freedom.

29801.q: Why was Uri particularly important for the king?
a: Because of the route over the Gotthard
29801.e: The route over the Gotthard to Italy ran through Uri. That is why the king took the valley under his direct rule in 1231.
29801.m: Uri was important because of the Gotthard.

29802.q: What did the people of Schwyz receive a charter of freedom from the emperor for in 1240?
a: For a victory in Swiss wrestling
29802.e: Warriors from Schwyz helped Emperor Frederick II during a siege in Italy. As thanks they were granted imperial freedom.
29802.m: Schwyz received its charter for helping in war.

29803.q: Which three places are called the Forest Cantons?
29803.e: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden lie on Lake Lucerne. They received charters of freedom early on and are seen as the core of the Confederation.
29803.m: The Forest Cantons are Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden.

29804.q: Whose rule was Uri freed from by its charter of freedom?
29804.e: Uri had previously been pledged to the Counts of Habsburg. The king bought the valley back and promised never to give it away again.
29804.m: The charter freed Uri from the Habsburgs.

29805.q: In which year was the Pact of Brunnen made?
29805.e: The charter is dated 9 December 1315. It renewed the older alliance of the Forest Cantons.
29805.m: The Pact of Brunnen dates from 1315.

29806.q: According to the Pact of Brunnen, what did the members have to give each other if one was attacked?
29806.e: If one member was attacked, the others had to help. Each member paid the costs of this help itself.
29806.m: In the Pact of Brunnen, the members promised each other help at their own expense.

29807.q: According to the Pact of Brunnen, what was nobody allowed to buy?
29807.e: Judges were not to be able to buy their office. Otherwise rich people could have bent the law to suit themselves.
29807.m: Nobody was allowed to buy the office of judge.

29808.q: Which word for the allies appears for the first time in the charter of Brunnen?
29808.e: The allies were bound to each other by an oath (“Eid”). That is why they called themselves companions of the oath.
29808.m: The word “Eidgenossen” (Confederates) appears for the first time in the Pact of Brunnen.

29809.q: According to the Pact of Brunnen, how were disputes between the members to be settled?
29809.e: Disputes between allies were not to be settled by force. People looked for mediators or went to court.
29809.m: Disputes between the members were settled by mediation and the law.

29810.q: According to the Pact of Brunnen, what was no member allowed to do without the agreement of the others?
29810.e: No member was to place itself under a lord or ally with outsiders on its own. This was meant to keep them united.
29810.m: No member could accept a foreign lord without the others.

29811.e: Brunnen lies in the canton of Schwyz on the shore of Lake Uri. This is part of Lake Lucerne.

29812.q: What title did the head of the town of Lucerne have in the Middle Ages?
29812.e: In Lucerne a Schultheiss (a kind of mayor) led the council. The title also existed in Bern and Solothurn.
29812.m: Lucerne was led by a Schultheiss.

29813.q: Compared with Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden, what was Lucerne in the alliance?
29813.e: The Forest Cantons were rural valley communities. With Lucerne, a town joined the alliance for the first time.
29813.m: Lucerne was the first town in the alliance.

29814.q: Whose rule did Lucerne belong to when it allied itself with the Forest Cantons?
29814.e: Lucerne was under Habsburg rule. The alliance with the Forest Cantons was therefore a brave step for the people of Lucerne.
29814.m: At that time Lucerne belonged to Habsburg.

29815.q: In which year did Lucerne ally itself with Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden?
29815.e: Lucerne made a perpetual alliance with the Forest Cantons in 1332. This brought the first town into the Confederation.

29816.q: How did goods from Lucerne usually travel on towards the Gotthard?
29816.e: There were hardly any roads along the steep lake shore. So goods were taken by boat to Flüelen and from there onwards by pack animals.
29816.m: From Lucerne, goods went by boat towards the Gotthard.

29817.q: Why was Lucerne particularly important for the Forest Cantons?
a: It was their most important market town
It lay right on the Rhine
29817.e: In Lucerne the farmers sold their cattle and bought grain and salt. The town also lay on the Gotthard route.
29817.m: Lucerne was the most important market of the Forest Cantons.

29818.q: Which famous wooden bridge in Lucerne was built around 1365?
29818.e: The Chapel Bridge was part of the town’s fortifications. It is one of the oldest covered wooden bridges in Europe.
29818.m: The Chapel Bridge in Lucerne dates from the 14th century.

29819.q: Which office in Zurich was Rudolf Brun the first to hold, in 1336?
29819.e: After the overthrow of the old council, an assembly elected Brun mayor for life. He was the first mayor of Zurich.
29819.m: Rudolf Brun was the first mayor of Zurich.

29820.q: Which groups got seats on the Zurich council through Rudolf Brun’s constitution?
29820.e: Brun’s guild constitution of 1336 divided the craftsmen into guilds. Their guild masters now sat on the council.
29820.m: Through Brun, the guilds entered the Zurich council.

29821.q: Which group gained a share in governing Zurich through the guild constitution of 1336?
29821.e: Before that, mainly rich merchants and nobles had ruled. Through Brun, the craftsmen entered the council via their guilds.
29821.m: Through Brun, the craftsmen helped govern Zurich.

29822.q: How long was Rudolf Brun to remain mayor of Zurich?
29822.e: After the overthrow of 1336, Brun was elected mayor for life. He ruled until his death in 1360.
29822.m: Rudolf Brun was mayor for life.

29823.q: Which lake is Zurich, the city Rudolf Brun ruled, on?
29823.e: Zurich lies at the lower end of Lake Zurich, where the Limmat flows out. Under Brun the city grew more powerful.

29824.q: With which places did Zurich make its perpetual alliance?
29824.e: Zurich allied itself with the three Forest Cantons and with Lucerne. This made the alliance bigger, reaching as far as the Limmat.
29824.m: Zurich allied itself with the Forest Cantons and Lucerne.

29825.q: In which century did Zurich join the Confederation?
29825.e: Zurich made a perpetual alliance with the Forest Cantons and Lucerne in 1351. That was in the 14th century.

29826.q: Why did Zurich seek an alliance with the Confederates?
a: It wanted to buy the Gotthard
It was looking for a new bishop
29826.e: Mayor Rudolf Brun had had Rapperswil destroyed, which belonged to a branch of the Habsburgs. Zurich therefore needed strong allies.
29826.m: Zurich allied itself with the Confederates against Habsburg.

29827.q: In which year did Bern join the Confederation?
29827.e: On 6 March 1353 Bern made a perpetual alliance. With this the powerful city became part of the Confederation.

29828.q: What number member of the Confederation did Bern become?
29828.e: Before Bern came Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Lucerne, Zurich, Glarus and Zug. Bern was the last of the old members of this period.

29829.q: With which places did Bern make a direct alliance in 1353?
29829.e: Bern allied itself with the three Forest Cantons. It was therefore linked to the other members only through them.
29829.m: In 1353 Bern allied itself with the three Forest Cantons.

29830.q: Why was Bern a particularly important new partner for the Confederates in 1353?
a: Bern was a large and powerful city
29830.e: Even then Bern had a large territory and a strong army. With Bern, the Confederation became much stronger.
29830.m: With Bern, a powerful city joined the alliance.

29831.q: How was Bern linked to Zurich and Lucerne after 1353?
a: Only indirectly through the Forest Cantons
Not at all, they were enemies
29831.e: The alliances of the Confederation were a web of separate treaties. Bern had a charter only with the Forest Cantons.
29831.m: Bern was linked to Zurich and Lucerne only through the Forest Cantons.

29832.q: How did Bern often enlarge its territory in the 14th century?
a: It inherited all of Habsburg’s land
It reclaimed land from Lake Thun
29832.e: Bern bought towns and lordships from nobles in debt, for example Burgdorf and Thun in 1384. This made its territory grow a lot.
29832.m: Bern often enlarged its territory by buying land.

29833.q: Until which year did Brun’s guild constitution essentially remain in force?
29833.e: The guild constitution lasted until the end of the Old Swiss Confederacy. Only the Helvetic Republic brought a new order.

29834.q: Which city won the Battle of Laupen in 1339?
29834.e: On 21 June 1339 Bern and its allies won at Laupen. Afterwards Bern became even more powerful.

29835.q: Which town fought against Bern at Laupen together with many nobles?
29835.e: Fribourg and the nobles of western Switzerland feared Bern’s growing power. That is why they marched against Bern together.
29835.m: Fribourg fought against Bern at Laupen.

29836.q: Who helped Bern in the Battle of Laupen?
29836.e: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden sent warriors to Laupen. Solothurn and some valley communities also helped Bern.
29836.m: The Forest Cantons helped Bern at Laupen.

29837.q: What did Bern’s enemies besiege before the Battle of Laupen?
29837.e: Fribourg and many nobles besieged Laupen. Bern came to help the town with its allies.
29837.m: Bern helped the besieged town of Laupen.

29838.q: Why did Fribourg and many nobles fight against Bern in 1339?
a: Bern wanted to elect a king
29838.e: Bern was becoming bigger and more powerful. Fribourg and the nobles of western Switzerland wanted to stop that.

29839.q: What did the victory at Laupen mean for Bern?
a: Bern could extend its power further
29839.e: After Laupen, Bern became the most important power in the west of what is now Switzerland. Agnes of Hungary negotiated the peace in 1340.
29839.m: After Laupen, Bern became even more powerful.

29840.q: In which battle is Arnold Winkelried said to have sacrificed himself?
29840.e: There the Confederates fought against a Habsburg army of knights. Winkelried’s deed is said to have made their victory possible.
29840.m: Winkelried is said to have sacrificed himself at Sempach.

29841.q: What is Winkelried said to have done in the battle?
a: He warned the army with a horn
29841.e: He is said to have gathered a bundle of lances into his arms and pulled them towards himself. This made a gap in the knights’ front line.
29841.m: Winkelried is said to have grabbed the enemy’s lances.

29842.q: Which place did the Winkelried family come from?
29842.e: The Winkelrieds were a family of knights from Nidwalden. They are recorded in this place from about 1250.

29843.q: What does Winkelried stand for in Swiss memory?
29843.e: Winkelried is said to have given his life so that his comrades could win. That is why he became a model of self-sacrifice.
29843.m: Winkelried is seen as a model of self-sacrifice.

29844.q: What does the famous Winkelried monument in Stans from 1865 show?
a: Winkelried with enemy lances in his arms
Winkelried with a crossbow and an apple
29844.e: The sculptor Ferdinand Schlöth showed Winkelried dying with the knights’ lances. The monument was unveiled in 1865.
29844.m: The Winkelried monument shows him with the enemy’s lances.

29845.q: Why do historians doubt that Winkelried really acted like this?
a: The deed is only mentioned much later
He only lived a hundred years afterwards
He fought on the other side
29845.e: The story first appears in a Zurich chronicle from around 1476, and there still without a name. No earlier source reports it.
29845.m: Winkelried’s deed is only mentioned long after the battle.

29846.q: Which famous sentence does the legend give to Winkelried?
a: “I will open a path for you”
29846.e: The “path” means the gap in the knights’ row of lances. The historian Johannes von Müller put the sentence into these words in 1805.
29846.m: Winkelried is said to have said: “I will open a path for you.”

29847.q: In which year did the Battle of Näfels take place?
29847.e: The battle was on 9 April 1388. Two years after Sempach, the people of Glarus defeated Habsburg.
29847.m: The Battle of Näfels was in 1388.

29848.q: Which place defended itself against Habsburg at Näfels?
29848.e: The people of Glarus wanted to free themselves from Habsburg rule. Supported by a few warriors from Central Switzerland, they won.
29848.m: At Näfels, the people of Glarus defeated Habsburg.

29849.e: Every year the people of Glarus walk in procession to the battle memorial. There the names of those who died are read out.
29849.m: The Näfelser Fahrt remembers the battle every year.

29850.q: In which season does the Näfelser Fahrt take place?
29850.e: The Näfelser Fahrt is on the first Thursday in April. The battle took place in April 1388.
29850.m: The Näfelser Fahrt is in April.

29851.q: Where did the people of Glarus get support from at Näfels?
29851.e: A few warriors from Central Switzerland helped the people of Glarus. Together they defeated the much larger Habsburg army.
29851.m: At Näfels, men from Central Switzerland helped the people of Glarus.

29852.q: Among other things, what did the people of Glarus use to defend themselves against the horsemen?
29852.e: From the slope, the people of Glarus threw stones at the disordered army. Many enemies fled and drowned near Weesen.
29852.m: The people of Glarus threw stones at the enemy horsemen.

29853.q: Roughly how many fighters faced each other at Näfels?
29853.e: The Confederates were heavily outnumbered. Even so, they lost only about 55 men, while the enemy lost around 1,700.
29853.m: At Näfels a small band defeated a much larger army.

29854.q: In which century was the Priests’ Charter (Pfaffenbrief) agreed?
29854.e: The Priests’ Charter was agreed in 1370. The year 1370 belongs to the 14th century.
29854.m: The Priests’ Charter dates from the 14th century.

29855.q: Who is meant by the word “Pfaffen” in the Priests’ Charter (Pfaffenbrief)?
29855.e: “Pfaffe” used to be a word for a priest or clergyman. The charter mainly set out their position.

29856.q: What did the Priests’ Charter lay down for clergymen?
a: They came under the local courts
They were not allowed to buy weapons
29856.e: In worldly disputes, clergymen could no longer appeal to foreign courts. Exceptions applied only to marriage and church matters.
29856.m: Clergymen also had to accept the local courts.

29857.q: What led to the Priests’ Charter in 1370?
29857.e: A Zurich clergyman attacked the Schultheiss of Lucerne and refused to accept a worldly court. After that, the members agreed the Priests’ Charter.
29857.m: An attack by a clergyman led to the Priests’ Charter.

29858.q: Who made the Priests’ Charter to make their territory safer?
29858.e: Zurich, Lucerne, Zug, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden agreed the Priests’ Charter in 1370. It ensured peace on the road to the Gotthard.
29858.m: Several members of the Confederation made the Priests’ Charter.

29859.q: Which route was the Priests’ Charter meant to make particularly safe?
a: The route from Zurich to the Gotthard
The route from Bern to Geneva
The route from Basel to Strasbourg
The route from Chur to Venice
29859.e: The members promised peace on the road from Zurich to the Gotthard. Safe roads were important for trade.
29859.m: The Priests’ Charter protected the route from Zurich to the Gotthard.

29861.q: According to the Sempach Charter, what were the warriors only allowed to do with their captains’ permission?
29861.e: Disorderly plundering put an army in danger. That is why permission from the leaders was needed.
29861.m: Plundering was only allowed with the captains’ permission.

29862.q: According to the Sempach Charter, which buildings were the warriors to spare?
29862.e: Churches and monasteries were not to be attacked or robbed. This applied even in enemy territory.
29862.m: Churches and monasteries had to be spared in war.

29863.e: In 1393 the eight members of the Confederation and Solothurn agreed on this shared set of rules.
29863.m: The Sempach Charter applied to the members of the Confederation.

29864.q: According to the Sempach Charter, which people were to be spared if they were not fighting?
29864.e: The charter banned attacks on women who were not taking part in the fighting. It was an early rule to protect the defenceless.
29864.m: Women who were not fighting had to be spared.

29865.q: According to the Sempach Charter, how was the spoils of war to be shared?
29865.e: Each member was to receive its share of the spoils. This was meant to avoid quarrels between the allies.
29865.m: The spoils were shared out proportionally.

29866.q: Whom did the people of Appenzell fight against at the start of the Appenzell Wars?
29866.e: The Abbey of St Gallen was the landlord in the Appenzell region and demanded high dues. The people of Appenzell resisted this.
29866.m: The people of Appenzell first resisted the Abbot of St Gallen.

29867.q: Where does the name Appenzell come from?
29867.e: The Latin name “abbatis cella” means the cell or estate of the abbot. It recalls the rule of the Abbey of St Gallen.
29867.m: Appenzell originally means cell of the abbot.

29868.q: Who won the Battle of Vögelinsegg in 1403?
29868.e: On 15 May 1403 the people of Appenzell put the army of the abbot and his allies to flight.
29868.m: The people of Appenzell won at Vögelinsegg.

29869.q: Whom did the people of Appenzell defeat in 1405 at the Battle of Stoss?
29869.e: Habsburg had come to help the abbot. At Stoss, the people of Appenzell successfully drove back this army.
29869.m: At Stoss, the people of Appenzell defeated a Habsburg army.

29870.q: The alliance of the people of Appenzell was called the “League above the Lake”. Around which lake were its members?
29870.e: The League above the Lake united Appenzell, the town of St Gallen and other places around Lake Constance. It fell apart in 1408.
29870.m: The League above the Lake lay around Lake Constance.

29871.q: What did the people of Appenzell achieve with the Appenzell Wars?
a: They became independent of the Abbot of St Gallen
They had to pay higher dues
29871.e: The people of Appenzell freed themselves from the rule of the Abbey of St Gallen. Later they became allies of the Confederates.
29871.m: The people of Appenzell freed themselves from the abbot’s rule.

29872.q: According to legend, which hero fought alone against many enemies at the Battle of Stoss?
29872.e: Uli Rotach is said to have leant against a hut and defeated several enemies. He is a folk hero of Appenzell.
29872.m: Uli Rotach is the hero of the Battle of Stoss.

29873.q: Which inheritance did Zurich and Schwyz quarrel over at the start of the Old Zurich War?
a: The inheritance of the Counts of Toggenburg
The inheritance of the Counts of Kyburg
The inheritance of the Dukes of Zähringen
The inheritance of the Counts of Habsburg
29873.e: Count Frederick VII of Toggenburg died in 1436 without children and without a will. Zurich and Schwyz both wanted his lands.
29873.m: The Old Zurich War began with the quarrel over the Toggenburg inheritance.

29874.q: Roughly when did the Old Zurich War take place?
29874.e: The war between Zurich and the other members of the Confederation lasted, with breaks, from 1440 to 1450.
29874.m: The Old Zurich War was a war in the middle of the 15th century.

29875.q: How was the Old Zurich War ended in 1450?
a: By the death of all the leaders
By an order from the Pope
29875.e: A court of arbitration under Heinrich von Bubenberg from Bern gave a ruling in 1450. After that there was peace again.
29875.m: An arbitration ruling ended the Old Zurich War in 1450.

29876.q: Which member of the Confederation was Zurich’s great opponent in the Old Zurich War?
29876.e: Zurich and Schwyz quarrelled over the Toggenburg inheritance. Schwyz was supported by the other members.
29876.m: In the Old Zurich War, Schwyz stood against Zurich.

29877.q: On which river outside Zurich did the people of Zurich fight the Confederates in 1443?
29877.e: The Battle of St Jakob an der Sihl took place right outside the city of Zurich. The Confederates won.
29877.m: In 1443 Zurich and the Confederates fought on the Sihl.

29878.q: What happened in 1444 in the so-called Murder of Greifensee?
a: The Confederates executed the defenders of the castle
Zurich destroyed the Abbey of Einsiedeln
An earthquake destroyed the little town
29878.e: After the siege of Greifensee, the Confederates had around 60 defenders beheaded. The deed was seen as cruel even at the time.
29878.m: In the Murder of Greifensee, the defenders were killed after surrendering.

29879.q: What did Zurich have to give up at the end of the Old Zurich War?
a: The right to have a mayor
29879.e: An arbitration ruling in 1450 forced Zurich to end its alliance with Habsburg. Zurich then remained part of the Confederation.
29879.m: After the war, Zurich returned to the alliance without its Habsburg pact.

29880.q: Why is the Old Zurich War seen as a special war in Swiss history?
a: It was the first war with cannons
It was fought entirely on the lake
It lasted only a single day
29880.e: In the Old Zurich War, one member of the Confederation fought against the others. That is why it is called a civil war within the alliance.
29880.m: The Old Zurich War was a war between fellow Confederates.

29881.q: In which century did the Battle of St Jakob an der Birs take place?
29881.e: The battle took place on 26 August 1444, so in the 15th century, during the Old Zurich War.
29881.m: The Battle of St Jakob an der Birs was in 1444.

29882.q: Outside which city is the battlefield of St Jakob an der Birs?
29882.e: St Jakob lies on the Birs at the edge of the city of Basel. Today there is a monument there, and the St. Jakob-Park stadium is nearby.
29882.m: St Jakob an der Birs is near Basel.

29883.q: What reminds people in Basel of the Battle of St Jakob an der Birs today?
29883.e: The St Jakob monument remembers the Confederates who fell. The St. Jakob-Park stadium is nearby today.
29883.m: A monument in Basel remembers the Battle of St Jakob.

29884.q: Which country did the large army come from that the Confederates fought at St Jakob an der Birs in 1444?
29884.e: The heir to the French throne led a huge army of mercenaries. These mercenaries were called the Armagnacs.
29884.m: At St Jakob, the Confederates fought against a French army.

29885.q: How did the Battle of St Jakob an der Birs end for the Confederates?
a: Almost all the Confederates were killed
29885.e: The small Confederate band fought against an army many times larger. In the end almost all the Confederates were dead.
29885.m: At St Jakob an der Birs the Confederates suffered a heavy defeat.

29886.q: Why did the French army still withdraw after the Battle of St Jakob?
a: It had suffered very heavy losses itself
It was driven away by a thunderstorm
The Pope ordered it to withdraw
29886.e: The Armagnacs suffered such heavy losses that the Dauphin gave up attacking the Confederation. Soon afterwards he made peace.
29886.m: The fierce resistance at St Jakob deterred the French.

29887.q: What did the Confederate troop at St Jakob an der Birs do against its leaders’ orders?
a: It crossed the Birs and attacked
29887.e: The troop was not supposed to advance across the Birs. It attacked the much larger army anyway.
29887.m: At St Jakob, the Confederates attacked against orders.

29888.q: Which territory did Charles the Bold rule?
29888.e: Charles the Bold was Duke of Burgundy. His realm stretched from the Netherlands to what is now western Switzerland.
29888.m: Charles the Bold was the Duke of Burgundy.

29889.q: What are the Confederates’ wars against Charles the Bold called?
29889.e: The Burgundian Wars lasted from 1474 to 1477. They ended with the death of Charles the Bold.
29889.m: The Confederates fought the Burgundian Wars against Charles the Bold.

29890.q: In which present-day country is Dijon, the old capital of Burgundy?
29890.e: Dijon was the capital of the Duchy of Burgundy. Charles the Bold was born there in 1433.
29890.m: Burgundy’s capital Dijon is in France today.

29891.q: What did Charles the Bold strive for but never achieve?
29891.e: Charles wanted to turn his duchy into a kingdom. But the emperor did not give him the crown.
29891.m: Charles the Bold wanted to become king.

29892.q: In which battle in 1476 did Charles the Bold lose to the Confederates?
29892.e: In 1476 the Confederates defeated Charles the Bold at Grandson and at Murten. In 1477 he was killed at Nancy.
29892.m: Charles the Bold lost to the Confederates at Murten in 1476.

29893.q: What happened to Charles the Bold at the Battle of Nancy in 1477?
a: He was killed in the battle
He made peace with the Confederates
29893.e: Duke René II of Lorraine defeated Charles outside Nancy with Swiss mercenaries. Charles was killed in the battle.
29893.m: Charles the Bold died at Nancy in 1477.

29894.q: What became of the Duchy of Burgundy after the death of Charles the Bold?
a: It was divided between France and Habsburg
It became part of the Confederation
29894.e: Charles’s daughter married a Habsburg. France took the duchy itself, and the Netherlands went to Habsburg.
29894.m: After Charles’s death, France and Habsburg divided his inheritance.

29895.q: In which present-day canton is Grandson?
29895.e: Grandson belongs to the canton of Vaud today. After the Burgundian Wars it was ruled jointly by Bern and Fribourg.
29895.m: Grandson is in the canton of Vaud.

29896.q: In which year did the Confederates defeat Charles the Bold at Grandson?
29896.e: The Battle of Grandson took place on 2 March 1476. The Battle of Murten followed in the same year.
29896.m: The Battle of Grandson was in March 1476.

29897.q: What made the Confederates furious shortly before the Battle of Grandson?
a: Charles had the garrison of Grandson executed
Charles burnt the city of Bern
Charles broke a truce with Uri
29897.e: The Confederate garrison of Grandson Castle had surrendered. Even so, Charles had the men hanged or drowned.
29897.m: The execution of the Grandson garrison made the Confederates furious.

29898.q: What did the Confederates capture after the Battle of Grandson?
29898.e: Charles’s army fled and left the camp behind. Tents, cannons, jewellery and tapestries fell into the hands of the victors.
29898.m: At Grandson the Confederates captured the Burgundian booty.

29899.q: Where can you see part of the Burgundian booty from the Burgundian Wars today?
a: In a national museum in Vienna
29899.e: Among other things, the Bern Historical Museum shows valuable Burgundian tapestries. They come from the booty of the Burgundian Wars.
29899.m: Many pieces of the Burgundian booty are in Bern today.

29900.q: Which saying came about after the Battle of Grandson?
a: At Grandson Charles lost his goods, at Murten his courage
At Grandson the victory is good for everyone
Whoever has Grandson also has Bern
29900.e: This well-known saying sums up Charles’s defeats. At Grandson he lost his treasures, at Murten his self-confidence.
29900.m: At Grandson Charles the Bold lost his goods.

29901.q: Whom did the Confederates fight at Murten in 1476?
29901.e: Charles the Bold besieged Murten. On 22 June 1476 the Confederates defeated him.
29901.m: At Murten the Confederates defeated Charles the Bold.

29902.q: Which man from Bern defended besieged Murten against Charles the Bold?
29902.e: Adrian von Bubenberg held the town of Murten with a small garrison until the Confederate relief army arrived.
29902.m: Adrian von Bubenberg held Murten against the Burgundians.

29903.q: How did the Battle of Murten end for Charles the Bold?
29903.e: The Burgundian army was crushed. Many Burgundians drowned in Lake Murten as they fled.
29903.m: At Murten Charles the Bold suffered a heavy defeat.

29904.q: What from the time of the Burgundian Wars is still well preserved in Murten today?
29904.e: The town wall protected Murten when Charles the Bold besieged it. You can still walk along it today.
29904.m: The town wall of Murten is still preserved today.

29905.q: According to legend, which tree is linked to the news of the victory at Murten?
a: The Murten lime tree in Fribourg
The fir tree of the Rütli
29905.e: A runner is said to have brought the news of the victory to Fribourg with a lime twig. The famous lime tree is said to have grown from it. The Murten run recalls this.
29905.m: The Murten lime tree recalls the legend of the victory runner.

29906.q: In which canton is the little town of Murten?
29906.e: Murten lies in the canton of Fribourg on Lake Murten. Its town wall is still well preserved today.
29906.m: Murten is in the canton of Fribourg.

29907.q: What did the priest of Stans do in 1481 when the Diet could not reach an agreement?
a: He went to Brother Klaus for advice
He called the emperor for help
29907.e: The priest hurried to the hermit Brother Klaus in the Ranft. He returned to Stans with his message, and the envoys reached an agreement.
29907.m: In 1481 the priest of Stans went to Brother Klaus for advice.

29908.q: What did rural members such as Uri and Schwyz fear before the Covenant of Stans?
a: That the towns would become too powerful
That the Gotthard would be closed
That the Pope would punish them
That their language would be banned
29908.e: The towns of Zurich, Bern and Lucerne wanted to admit Fribourg and Solothurn. The rural members feared that the towns would then have the majority.
29908.m: The rural members feared the power of the towns.

29909.q: Between which groups was there a quarrel before the Covenant of Stans?
a: Between town members and rural members
29909.e: The rural members such as Uri and Schwyz feared that the towns would become too powerful. There was also a quarrel about the Burgundian booty.
29909.m: Before 1481 the town and rural members quarrelled with each other.

29910.q: In which present-day canton is Stans, where the Covenant of Stans was made?
29910.e: Stans is the capital of the canton of Nidwalden. The envoys of the members met there in December 1481.
29910.m: Stans is the capital of Nidwalden.

29911.q: Whose advice helped the Diet in Stans to reach an agreement after all?
29911.e: The priest of Stans went to the hermit Niklaus von Flüe for advice. His message helped to settle the quarrel.
29911.m: Brother Klaus helped bring about the agreement in Stans in 1481.

29912.q: Among other things, what did the Covenant of Stans set out?
a: How spoils of war were shared
29912.e: The agreement laid down how spoils and conquered lands were to be shared. The members were also not allowed to stir up each other’s subjects.
29912.m: The Covenant of Stans set out how the spoils were shared.

29913.q: What did the Covenant of Stans oblige the members to do if subjects rebelled?
29913.e: The members promised to support each other during uprisings in their territories. This strengthened the authorities in towns and rural areas.
29913.m: The members helped each other against uprisings.

29914.q: By which name is Niklaus von Flüe also known?
29914.e: Niklaus von Flüe lived as a hermit, and the people called him “Brother Klaus”.
29914.m: Niklaus von Flüe is popularly called Brother Klaus.

29915.q: Where did Niklaus von Flüe live as a hermit?
29915.e: He lived in a small cell in the Ranft gorge near Flüeli in the canton of Obwalden. The place is a site of pilgrimage today.
29915.m: Brother Klaus lived in the Ranft in Obwalden.

29916.q: How many children did Niklaus von Flüe have with his wife Dorothea Wyss?
29916.e: Niklaus and Dorothea had ten children. Only at the age of 50, as a father, did he withdraw to live as a hermit.

29917.q: Which offices did Niklaus von Flüe hold before he became a hermit?
29917.e: Niklaus was a respected farmer, councillor and judge. He is said to have turned down the office of Landammann.
29917.m: Brother Klaus was first a farmer and councillor in Obwalden.

29919.q: What is told about what Brother Klaus ate in the Ranft?
a: He is said to have lived for about 20 years without food
He is said to have eaten only fish
He is said to have had only bread and wine
He is said to have lived on herbs
29919.e: According to tradition, Brother Klaus lived for about 20 years without food. People of his own time already reported this.
29919.m: It is reported that Brother Klaus fasted for years.

29920.q: Which piece of advice is attributed to Niklaus von Flüe?
a: Do not make the fence too wide
One for all, all for one
29920.e: The saying “Do not make the fence too wide” is often understood as advice against conquests. It is not certain whether it really comes from Brother Klaus.
29920.m: Brother Klaus is said to have warned against conquering too much.

29921.q: In which century did Niklaus von Flüe live?
29921.e: Niklaus von Flüe was born in 1417 and died in 1487. So he lived in the 15th century.
29921.m: Brother Klaus lived in the 15th century.

29922.q: In which year did the Swabian War take place?
29922.e: The Swabian War was fought in 1499. It lasted only from January to September.

29923.q: Whom did the Confederates fight in the Swabian War?
a: The Swabian League and the Habsburgs
29923.e: In the Swabian War, the Confederates fought against King Maximilian of the House of Habsburg and the Swabian League. They won several battles.
29923.m: In the Swabian War the Confederates fought against Habsburg and the Swabian League.

29924.q: Which battle in the canton of Solothurn decided the Swabian War in July 1499?
29924.e: On 22 July 1499 the Confederates won at Dornach. Peace negotiations soon followed.
29924.m: The Battle of Dornach decided the Swabian War.

29925.q: Which peace ended the Swabian War?
29925.e: The Peace of Basel was made on 22 September 1499. The Duke of Milan helped to negotiate it.
29925.m: The Swabian War ended in 1499 with the Peace of Basel.

29926.q: What important result did the Swabian War have for the Confederation?
a: It broke away from the Holy Roman Empire in practice
29926.e: After 1499 the imperial court and imperial taxes no longer really applied to the Confederates. Legally they only left the empire in 1648.
29926.m: After the Swabian War the Confederation was largely independent of the empire.

29927.q: Which allies of the Confederates fought in the Grisons during the Swabian War?
29927.e: The Three Leagues in the Grisons were allies of the Confederates. At the Calven they defeated the Habsburg army in 1499.
29927.m: People from the Grisons also fought in the Swabian War.

29928.q: Which two cities became members of the Confederation in 1501, shortly after the Swabian War?
29928.e: Basel and Schaffhausen joined the alliance in 1501. They lay close to the border with the empire and were looking for protection.
29928.m: Basel and Schaffhausen joined the Confederation in 1501.

29929.q: What is the Swabian War often called in Germany and Austria?
29929.e: Each side named the war after its enemy. That is why people in southern Germany and Austria called it the Swiss War.
29929.m: On the other side, the Swabian War is called the Swiss War.

a: A mercenary serving a foreign power
29930.e: Reisläufer were Swiss men who fought in foreign armies for pay. The word comes from “Reise”, which at that time meant a military campaign.
29930.m: A Reisläufer fought in foreign armies for money.

29931.q: What did the word “Reise” in the term Reisläufer originally mean?
29931.e: In the Middle Ages, “Reise” meant a military campaign. Anyone who “ran into the Reise” went to war.

29932.q: In connection with mercenaries, what were pensions?
a: Payments by foreign princes to cantons and politicians
29932.e: Foreign rulers paid money to members of the Confederation and to influential men so that they could recruit mercenaries. These payments were called pensions.
29932.m: With pensions, foreign princes bought the right to recruit mercenaries.

29933.q: Which weapon was typical of the closely packed formations of Swiss mercenaries?
29933.e: The Confederates fought in tight formations with long pikes and halberds. This let them fight off cavalry attacks.
29933.m: Swiss mercenaries often fought with the pike.

29934.q: Which reformer in Zurich fought against mercenary service?
29934.e: Zwingli had seen the horrors of the mercenary wars himself. He condemned mercenary service and the pensions.
29934.m: Zwingli was a fierce opponent of mercenary service.

29935.q: Why did many young men go abroad as mercenaries in the 15th and 16th centuries?
a: There was little work and pay at home
They had to join the emperor’s army
They wanted to learn foreign languages
It was required by law for farmers
29935.e: Many valleys were poor and could not feed everyone. The pay and the hope of booty drew the men into foreign armies.
29935.m: Poverty drove many young Confederates into mercenary service.

29936.q: Which Pope founded the Pontifical Swiss Guard?
29936.e: Pope Julius II brought Swiss mercenaries to Rome in 1506. They were to protect him and the Vatican.
29936.m: Pope Julius II founded the Swiss Guard.

29938.q: What happened on 6 May 1527 during the Sack of Rome?
a: Many guards were killed protecting the Pope
29938.e: Troops of Emperor Charles V plundered Rome. Most of the guards were killed, while the Pope was able to escape to Castel Sant’Angelo.
29938.m: During the Sack of Rome, the guards saved the Pope at great cost.

29939.q: Why are new Swiss Guards sworn in every year on 6 May?
a: In memory of the Sack of Rome
Because it is the Pope’s birthday
Because Easter falls on that day
Because Switzerland was founded on that day
29939.e: On 6 May 1527 the Guard defended the Pope. The swearing-in takes place on this day in memory of it.
29939.m: The guards take their oath on 6 May.

29940.q: Where does the Pontifical Swiss Guard serve?
a: In the Federal Palace in Bern
29940.e: The Swiss Guard protects the Pope in the Vatican. The Vatican is a small state in the middle of Rome.
29940.m: The Swiss Guard serves in the Vatican.

29941.q: Who can become a Swiss Guard (as of 2025)?
a: A young Catholic Swiss man with military training
29941.e: Applicants must be Swiss citizens, Catholic, single and between 19 and 30 years old (as of 2025). They need to have done Swiss basic military training and be at least 174 cm tall.
29941.m: Guards are young Swiss men who have done basic military training.

29942.q: Which traditional weapon do Swiss Guards carry with their parade uniform?
29942.e: The halberd is a pole weapon with an axe blade and a point. It was the typical weapon of Confederate warriors, and the Guard still carries it today.
29942.m: The Swiss Guard still carries the halberd today.

29943.q: Which territory did France and the Confederates fight over in the Milanese wars?
29943.e: France, Habsburg, Venice, the Pope and the Confederates all wanted influence over the rich Duchy of Milan. The Confederates often fought as mercenaries and for their own gain.
29943.m: The Milanese wars were about who ruled Milan.

29944.q: Which town in Ticino with three castles passed to Uri, Schwyz and Nidwalden in 1500?
29944.e: Bellinzona guarded the route from the Gotthard to the south. Its three castles are a UNESCO World Heritage Site today.
29944.m: Bellinzona passed to three original Swiss cantons in 1500.

29945.q: Who defeated the Confederates at the Battle of Marignano?
29945.e: Francis I had only just become king. With strong cavalry, cannons and help from Venice, he defeated the Confederates.
29945.m: Francis I of France won at Marignano in 1515.

29946.q: How did the Battle of Marignano in 1515 end for the Confederates?
29946.e: At Marignano the Confederates lost to France. Afterwards they largely gave up their conquests in Italy.
29946.m: Marignano in 1515 was a heavy defeat for the Confederates.

29947.q: How did many Confederates fight in the Milanese wars?
29947.e: Many Confederates went to Italy as mercenaries. Foreign rulers paid them for military service.
29947.m: Many Confederates fought as mercenaries in Italy.

29948.q: Which present-day canton’s territory did the Confederates gain through the Milanese wars?
29948.e: Lugano, Locarno and other areas south of the Alps came under Confederate rule. They were governed as bailiwicks beyond the mountains.
29948.m: Through the Milanese wars, Ticino came to the Confederation.

29949.q: Which future reformer was at Marignano as an army chaplain?
29949.e: Zwingli went with the troops from Glarus to Italy as their chaplain. His experiences made him an opponent of mercenary service.
29949.m: Zwingli lived through the Milanese wars as an army chaplain.

29950.q: Where is Marignano, where the Confederates fought in 1515?
29950.e: Marignano is called Melegnano today and lies south-east of Milan. The Confederates lost to France there in 1515.
29950.m: Marignano is near Milan in northern Italy.

29951.q: What did France and the Confederates promise each other in the Perpetual Peace of 1516?
a: Never to wage war against each other again
29951.e: Both sides agreed never to fight against each other again. That is where the name “Perpetual Peace” comes from.
29951.m: In the Perpetual Peace both sides promised lasting peace.

29952.q: After which battle did France and the Confederates make the Perpetual Peace in 1516?
29952.e: In 1515 the Confederates lost to France at Marignano. A year later both sides made the Perpetual Peace.
29952.m: The Perpetual Peace followed Marignano in 1516.

29953.q: Until when did the Perpetual Peace between France and the Confederation last?
29953.e: The treaty had no end date and lasted almost 300 years. Only the invasion by French troops in 1798 ended it.
29953.m: The Perpetual Peace lasted until the French invasion of 1798.

29954.q: What else did the Confederates receive from France with the Perpetual Peace?
a: Payments of money and trade advantages
A seat in the French parliament
29954.e: France paid large sums and yearly pensions to the members of the Confederation. The Confederates also received trade advantages in Milan and Lyon.
29954.m: France paid the Confederates for the peace.

29955.q: Which agreement with France followed the Perpetual Peace in 1521?
29955.e: In the mercenary alliance of 1521, the members allowed France to recruit mercenaries. Zurich did not take part, under Zwingli’s influence.
29955.m: From 1521 the Confederates supplied France with mercenaries.

29956.q: Why was the Perpetual Peace important for Swiss mercenaries?
a: Many then served in the army of the French kings
It created a Swiss army in Paris
It sent all mercenaries to Rome
29956.e: France became the most important employer of Swiss mercenaries. Swiss regiments served the French kings until the Revolution.
29956.m: After 1516 many Swiss fought for France.

29957.q: Which claim did the Confederates in effect give up in the Perpetual Peace?
a: The claim to be Milan’s protector
29957.e: After Marignano the Confederates gave up their claim to protect and control Milan. But they kept the bailiwicks in Ticino.
29957.m: In the Perpetual Peace the Confederates gave up Milan.

29958.q: Which common lordship lay on the Rhine in what is now the canton of St Gallen?
29958.e: From the late 15th century, the Rhine Valley was ruled jointly by several members of the Confederation. The Sargans region was also a common lordship.
29958.m: The Rhine Valley was a common lordship.

29959.q: Who governed a common lordship on the spot?
29959.e: The ruling members took turns to appoint a bailiff. He usually held office for two years.
29959.m: A common lordship was governed by a bailiff.

29960.q: Which territory did the Confederates conquer in 1460 and then govern jointly?
29960.e: In 1460 the Confederates conquered Habsburg-ruled Thurgau. It remained a common lordship until 1798.
29960.m: Thurgau was a common lordship of the Confederates.

29961.q: Which territory did the Confederates conquer from the Habsburgs in 1415?
29961.e: In 1415 the Confederates conquered Aargau. Parts of it, such as the County of Baden, were then ruled jointly.

29962.q: What rights did the people in the common lordships have towards the ruling members?
a: They were subjects with no say in the alliance
They had their own vote at the Diet
29962.e: The inhabitants were subjects of the ruling members. They had no say in the Diet.
29962.m: The people in the common lordships were subjects.

29963.q: When did the common lordships come to an end?
a: In 1481 with the Covenant of Stans
29963.e: When France invaded in 1798, the Helvetic Republic was created. The subject territories were freed and later became cantons.
29963.m: In 1798 the subjects of the common lordships were freed.

29964.q: Which present-day canton used to consist of common lordships south of the Alps?
29964.e: Areas such as Lugano and Locarno were governed for a long time by Confederate bailiffs. In 1803 they became the canton of Ticino.
29964.m: Ticino used to consist of common lordships.

29965.q: What was the Diet (Tagsatzung) in the Old Swiss Confederacy?
a: The assembly of envoys from the members
29965.e: Envoys from the members of the Confederation met at the Diet. They discussed shared questions such as war, peace and subject territories.
29965.m: The Diet was the meeting of envoys from all the members.

29966.q: In which town did the Diet meet particularly often in the 15th and 16th centuries?
29966.e: Baden lay in a common lordship and was easy to reach. That is why a great many Diets were held there.
29966.m: The Diet often met in Baden.

29967.q: What did the envoys take home after a Diet?
29967.e: The decisions of the Diet were written down. The envoys took them to their members, who then decided on them.
29967.m: The Diet’s decisions were written down and taken back to the members.

29968.q: Why could the Diet not simply give orders to the members?
a: The envoys needed instructions from their members
It met only every ten years
29968.e: The envoys were bound by the instructions of their authorities. Important decisions applied only if the members agreed.
29968.m: The Diet was not a government with power of its own.

29969.q: How many members did the Confederation have after Appenzell joined in 1513?
29969.e: With Appenzell in 1513, the Confederation consisted of 13 members. It stayed that way until 1798.
29969.m: From 1513 there were the 13 old members.

29970.q: Until which year did the Diet exist as the assembly of the members?
29970.e: With the Federal Constitution of 1848, the Diet was replaced by the parliament with the National Council and the Council of States.
29970.m: The Diet ended with the Federal Constitution of 1848.

29971.q: Which allies of the Confederation did not have full rights at the Diet?
29971.e: Associates such as the town of St Gallen or Valais were allied with the Confederation. But they were not full members.
29971.m: Associates were allies without full rights.

29972.q: What started the First War of Kappel in 1529?
a: A Protestant pastor was burnt in Schwyz
29972.e: The pastor Jakob Kaiser was captured in Schwyz and burnt as a heretic. Zurich then marched against the Catholic members.
29972.m: The execution of a Protestant pastor led to the First War of Kappel.

29973.q: According to legend, which food did both sides in the war eat together in 1529?
29973.e: According to tradition, men from Central Switzerland put a pot of milk on the border and men from Zurich added bread. This created the famous Kappel milk soup as a sign of reconciliation.
29973.m: The Kappel milk soup stands for reconciliation between Confederates.

29974.q: Which reformer from Zurich was killed in 1531 at the Battle of Kappel?
29974.e: Huldrych Zwingli went with the Zurich troops as their chaplain and was killed on 11 October 1531 at Kappel am Albis.
29974.m: Zwingli died in 1531 at the Battle of Kappel.

29975.q: Where is Kappel, which gave its name to the Wars of Kappel?
a: On the Albis in the canton of Zurich
On the Brünig in the canton of Bern
On the Gotthard in the canton of Uri
On the Rhine in the canton of Basel
29975.e: Kappel am Albis lies in the canton of Zurich near the border with the canton of Zug. The armies of both faiths faced each other there.
29975.m: Kappel am Albis lies on the border between Zurich and Zug.

29976.q: What means of pressure did Zurich use in 1531 to try to force the Catholic members?
29976.e: Zurich and Bern imposed a blockade on supplies of grain and salt. The members from Central Switzerland responded with an attack.
29976.m: A food blockade started the Second War of Kappel.

29977.q: Who won the Second War of Kappel in 1531?
29977.e: The five Catholic members defeated Zurich and its allies. After that, the Reformation could not spread any further in the Confederation.
29977.m: The Catholic members won the Second War of Kappel.

29978.q: What did the Second Peace of Kappel of 1531 lay down?
a: Each member decides its own faith
29978.e: The peace treaty let each member choose its own faith. As a result, the Confederation stayed divided by religion for a long time.
29978.m: After 1531 each member decided its faith for itself.

29979.q: Which members formed the Catholic side against Zurich in 1531?
29979.e: The five inner members Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Zug kept the old faith. They fought together against Protestant Zurich.
29979.m: The five inner members stayed Catholic.

29980.q: How many Wars of Kappel were there?
29980.e: The First War of Kappel in 1529 ended without a battle, with the milk soup. In the Second War of Kappel in 1531, the Catholic members won at Kappel and at the Gubel.
29980.m: There were two Wars of Kappel, in 1529 and 1531.

29981.q: In which period did the Disputation of Baden take place?
a: In the time of the Helvetic Republic
29981.e: The disputation took place in Baden in 1526. At that time Catholics and Protestants argued about the true faith.
29981.m: The Disputation of Baden was a religious debate of the Reformation period.

29982.e: In a disputation, scholars argue their views in an orderly debate. In the Reformation period, it was about questions of faith.
29982.m: A disputation is an orderly debate.

29983.q: Which side did the theologian Johannes Eck represent at the Disputation of Baden?
29983.e: Johannes Eck from Ingolstadt was a well-known opponent of Luther and Zwingli. In Baden he spoke for the Catholic Church.
29983.m: Johannes Eck spoke for the Catholic side in Baden.

29984.q: Which city did Johannes Oecolampadius, who spoke for the Reformation in Baden, come from?
29984.e: Johannes Oecolampadius was the reformer of Basel. He represented the new teaching in Baden because Zwingli did not come.
29984.m: Oecolampadius was the reformer of Basel.

29985.q: Why did Zwingli not travel to the Disputation of Baden?
a: He was already living in Geneva
He was still Catholic at the time
29985.e: Zwingli did not trust the Catholic members and was afraid of being arrested or killed. That is why Zurich did not let him go to Baden.
29985.m: Zwingli stayed away from Baden because he feared for his life.

29986.q: Which side was declared the winner in Baden in 1526?
29986.e: The majority of the Diet declared the Catholic side the winner. Zwingli and his teaching were condemned.
29986.m: In Baden the Catholic side was declared the winner.

29987.q: Which city introduced the Reformation after holding its own disputation in 1528?
29987.e: After the Disputation of Baden, Bern held its own religious debate in 1528. After that Bern became Protestant, which made the Protestants strong.
29987.m: Bern became Protestant in 1528 after the Bern Disputation.

29988.q: Who mainly organised the Disputation of Baden?
29988.e: The Diet, with its Catholic majority, invited people to Baden and set the rules. Baden was a common lordship and a usual meeting place of the Confederates.
29988.m: The Catholic cantons called the meeting in Baden in 1526.

29989.q: Whose successor did Heinrich Bullinger become in Zurich in 1531?
29989.e: After Zwingli's death at Kappel, Bullinger became minister at the Grossmünster at the end of 1531. He led the Zurich church for over 40 years.

29990.q: In which church did Heinrich Bullinger preach in Zurich?
29990.e: Like Zwingli before him, Bullinger was minister at the Grossmünster. From there he led the Zurich church for over 40 years.

29991.q: Heinrich Bullinger was born in Bremgarten in 1504. In which present-day canton is Bremgarten?
29991.e: Bremgarten is a small town on the river Reuss in the canton of Aargau. Bullinger's father was a priest there.
29991.m: Bullinger came from Bremgarten in Aargau.

29992.q: What is Heinrich Bullinger's “Second Helvetic Confession”?
a: A summary of the Reformed faith
A peace treaty with the Habsburgs
A law book of the city of Zurich
29992.e: In it Bullinger wrote down what Reformed Christians believe. It appeared in 1566 and was accepted by Reformed churches in many countries.
29992.m: The Second Helvetic Confession sums up the Reformed faith.

29993.q: With which Geneva reformer did Bullinger reach agreement on Holy Communion in 1549?
29993.e: In the Zurich Agreement (Consensus Tigurinus) of 1549, Bullinger and Calvin came to an agreement. This brought the churches of Zurich and Geneva closer together.
29993.m: Bullinger and Calvin reached agreement in 1549.

29994.q: What is Heinrich Bullinger especially famous for among historians?
29994.e: Around 12,000 of Bullinger's letters have survived. He was in contact with scholars and princes all over Europe.
29994.m: Bullinger wrote thousands of letters all over Europe.

29995.q: Why did Protestants from Locarno have to leave their home and move to Zurich in 1555?
a: Because they were not allowed to stay in Catholic Locarno
Because an earthquake destroyed the town
Because they found work as fishermen in Zurich
Because Locarno was sold to Italy
29995.e: The Catholic cantons that ruled Locarno would not tolerate the Protestants. Zurich took them in under Bullinger, and some of them set up silk businesses there.
29995.m: In 1555 Zurich took in Protestant refugees from Locarno.

29996.q: What job did Heinrich Bullinger have in Zurich for over 40 years?
a: He was mayor of the city
29996.e: As Antistes, Bullinger was the chief minister of the Zurich church. He held this office from 1531 until his death in 1575.
29996.m: Bullinger led the Zurich church for over 40 years.

29997.q: What were the French Protestants called?
29997.e: Calvin's followers in France were called Huguenots. Because they were persecuted, many fled to Reformed areas such as Geneva.
29997.m: The French Protestants were called Huguenots.

29998.q: What happened in Paris on St Bartholomew's Night in 1572?
a: A great fire destroyed the city
29998.e: On St Bartholomew's Night, 24 August 1572, thousands of Huguenots were killed in Paris. Afterwards many survivors fled to Geneva.
29998.m: After St Bartholomew's Night in 1572, many Huguenots fled to Geneva.

29999.q: What did the Edict of Nantes of 1598 allow the Huguenots in France to do?
29999.e: King Henry IV issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598. It gave the Huguenots freedom of religion until Louis XIV cancelled it in 1685.
29999.m: From 1598 the Edict of Nantes protected the Huguenots.

30001.q: Which craft did Huguenot refugees especially promote in Geneva?
30001.e: Many Huguenots were skilled craftsmen and merchants. They helped Geneva become a centre of watchmaking.
30001.m: Huguenots helped to build up Geneva's watchmaking.

30003.q: Why was Geneva also called the “Protestant Rome”?
a: Because it was a centre of the Reformed faith
Because it lies on seven hills
30003.e: Geneva meant to many Reformed Christians what Rome meant to Catholics: the most important centre for many Reformed Christians. Ministers were trained here and sent to other countries.
30003.m: Geneva counted as the Protestant Rome.

30004.q: In which year did the Escalade of Geneva take place?
30004.e: On the night of 11 to 12 December 1602, Savoyard troops tried to capture Geneva. The attack failed.
30004.m: The Escalade of Geneva was in 1602.

30006.q: What does the French word “escalade” mean?
30006.e: The Savoyard soldiers wanted to climb the city walls secretly at night. That is where the name Escalade comes from.
30006.m: Escalade means climbing up the walls.

30007.q: What did the Savoyard soldiers use to get over the walls of Geneva in 1602?
30007.e: The attackers brought ladders painted black so they could climb the walls at night without being seen. Some got in, but they were driven back.
30007.m: The Savoyards climbed the walls with ladders.

30008.q: According to legend, which woman of Geneva poured hot soup on an attacker?
30008.e: Catherine Cheynel, known as Mère Royaume, is said to have thrown a pot of hot vegetable soup at a soldier. She became the heroine of the Escalade.
30008.m: Mère Royaume fought back with a soup pot.

30009.q: Which sweet treat is part of the Escalade festival today?
a: A chocolate pot with marzipan vegetables
30009.e: In memory of Mère Royaume, a chocolate pot is smashed. Inside are little vegetables made of marzipan.
30009.m: At the Escalade people smash a chocolate pot.

30010.q: Which public race takes place in Geneva's old town every year at the Escalade?
30010.e: The Course de l'Escalade runs through Geneva's old town. Many runners take part in fancy dress.
30010.m: The Course de l'Escalade race is part of the Escalade.

30011.q: In which month does Geneva celebrate the Escalade every year?
30011.e: The attack was on the night of 11 to 12 December 1602. That is why the Escalade is celebrated every December.
30011.m: The Escalade is celebrated in December.

30012.q: At what time of day did the Savoyard soldiers attack Geneva in 1602?
30012.e: The soldiers came in the dark so that nobody would notice them. Even so, the people of Geneva woke up in time and fought back.
30012.m: The Savoyards attacked Geneva at night.

30013.q: Which city did Johann Rudolf Wettstein come from?
30013.e: Wettstein was born in Basel in 1594 and later became mayor of the city. He is seen as an important diplomat of the Swiss Confederation.

30014.q: Which office did Wettstein hold in his home city from 1645?
30014.e: Wettstein became mayor of Basel in 1645. In this role he travelled to the peace negotiations in Westphalia.
30014.m: Wettstein was mayor of Basel from 1645.

30015.q: Which war ended in 1648 with the Peace of Westphalia?
30015.e: The Thirty Years' War devastated large parts of Central Europe from 1618 to 1648. The Swiss Confederation was largely spared.
30015.m: The Peace of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years' War in 1648.

30016.q: What did Wettstein achieve for the Swiss Confederation in 1648?
a: Independence from the Holy Roman Empire
The founding of the federal state
30016.e: In the Peace of Westphalia the Confederation was freed from the Empire. This made it a legally independent state as well.
30016.m: Since 1648 the Confederation has been independent of the Empire.

30017.q: Johann Rudolf Wettstein was a diplomat. What does a diplomat do?
a: Negotiates with other states for their country
30017.e: From 1646 to 1648 Wettstein negotiated for the Confederates in Münster in Westphalia with the Emperor's envoys.
30017.m: As a diplomat, Wettstein negotiated for the Swiss Confederation.

30018.q: What changed for Basel merchants in 1648 because of independence from the Empire?
a: Imperial courts could no longer judge them
They no longer had to pay taxes
They were no longer allowed to travel to Germany
30018.e: Wettstein's mission began because of lawsuits against Basel merchants at the Imperial Chamber Court. Once free of the Empire, that court no longer had any say.
30018.m: After 1648 imperial courts had no power over the Confederates.

30019.q: Which river does the Wettstein Bridge in Basel cross?
30019.e: The Wettstein Bridge links Grossbasel with Kleinbasel. Wettsteinplatz also reminds people of the mayor.
30019.m: The Wettstein Bridge honours Johann Rudolf Wettstein.

30020.q: What was Basel's religion in the time of Johann Rudolf Wettstein?
30020.e: Basel had been Reformed since 1529. In 1646 Wettstein first travelled to Westphalia on behalf of the Reformed cantons.
30020.m: Basel was Reformed in Wettstein's time.

30021.q: In which year did the great Swiss Peasants' War take place?
30021.e: The Swiss Peasants' War broke out in 1653. It was the biggest uprising of country people in the Old Swiss Confederacy.
30021.m: The Swiss Peasants' War was in 1653.

30022.q: In which valley in Lucerne did the Peasants' War of 1653 begin?
30022.e: The peasants of the Entlebuch were the first to rise up against the city of Lucerne. The uprising then spread to Bern, Solothurn and Basel.
30022.m: The Peasants' War began in the Entlebuch.

30023.q: Which Bernese farmer was the most important leader in the Peasants' War of 1653?
30023.e: Niklaus Leuenberger from Rüderswil in the Emmental was elected leader of the peasants. He led the negotiations with the cities.
30023.m: Niklaus Leuenberger led the peasants in 1653.

30024.q: What made things much worse for the peasants before 1653?
30024.e: After the Thirty Years' War, prices for farm produce fell. On top of that, Bern and Lucerne devalued their Batzen coins, so the peasants' savings were worth less.
30024.m: Falling prices and devalued coins drove the peasants to rise up.

30025.q: What did the rebel peasants do in Huttwil in May 1653?
